quote: An explosive critique of early 19th-century agrarian policy disguised as a story about a hungry caterpillar.
Moby-Dick is, at its heart, a 600-page plea for better maritime HR practices.
Goodnight Moon is the most chilling surveillance thriller of the century. Note how nothing in that room escapes being catalogued.
Hamlet is a gripping workplace drama about a man who simply cannot reply to an email.
Pride and Prejudice: a sweeping epic about real estate, with some dancing to pad the page count.
Green Eggs and Ham dismantles the entire food-safety regulatory apparatus in under 800 words. Terrifying.
The Giving Tree is the only honest book ever written about venture capital.
The Great Gatsby is a cautionary tale about what happens when you throw parties without checking the RSVPs.
The Hobbit is a searing indictment of unsolicited dinner guests and the collapse of the pantry-based economy.
Frankenstein is a gentle romantic comedy about a man who should have read the terms and conditions.
War and Peace is mostly a very long seating chart with occasional cannon fire.
1984 is a cozy domestic story about a man who just wants a quiet room and a nice diary.
Lord of the Flies is the definitive guide to group project dynamics.
The Odyssey is a ten-year travel blog by a man who refuses to ask for directions.
Little Women is a tense corporate thriller about four sisters fighting over one Christmas budget.
Charlotte's Web is the most effective PR campaign in agricultural history.
The Road is an aspirational van-life memoir. Light on amenities, big on vibes.
Don Quixote is about a man who took a LinkedIn post about slaying your dragons far too literally.
The Catcher in the Rye is a three-day Yelp review of New York City.
Jane Eyre is a property-disclosure horror story. Always ask about the attic.
Alice in Wonderland is a scathing exposé of unregulated food and beverage labeling.
Crime and Punishment is 500 pages of a man overthinking a text he already sent.
Where the Wild Things Are follows a boy who got sent to his room and came out with a startup.
The Cat in the Hat is a cautionary tale about letting a consultant into your house.
Of Mice and Men is the best book ever written about a roommate's big plans for rabbits.
Dracula is the story of a landlord who absolutely will not stop texting.
The Old Man and the Sea is a brutal one-star review of a fishing charter.
Romeo and Juliet is a three-day situationship that got wildly out of hand.
The Little Prince is a sharp critique of a portfolio concentrated in exactly one rose.
Robinson Crusoe is the original "taking some time for myself" post.
The Metamorphosis is a workplace story about a man whose boss is mainly upset he missed the 7am train.
Ulysses is the single greatest novel ever written about running errands.
Pinocchio is a gripping legal drama about the admissibility of nasal evidence.
The Giver is about a guy who finally finds the color settings.
Treasure Island is a sobering look at what happens when you crowdsource a retirement plan.
Sense and Sensibility is two sisters sharing one Notes app full of red flags.
Heart of Darkness is a corporate offsite that went extremely off-agenda.
Animal Farm is the most accurate set of HOA meeting minutes ever published.
Peter Pan is about a man who never moved out of his college town, and honestly, respect.
Harry Potter is seven books about a boy who gets into an elite school on a legacy admission.
The Hunger Games is the most thorough critique of reality TV casting practices ever written.
The Three Little Pigs is a dense treatise on residential building codes.
Goldilocks and the Three Bears is the first recorded Airbnb dispute.
The Raven is about a man haunted by a bird with exactly one talking point.
Gulliver's Travels is a frequent-flyer memoir in which every lounge is the wrong size.
Waiting for Godot is two hours of men waiting for the group chat organizer to show up.
The Tortoise and the Hare is a pointed critique of sprinting a marathon after one spin class.
The Scarlet Letter is the first recorded case of a personal brand going viral.
Great Expectations is the definitive text on networking upward.
The Wizard of Oz is an exposé of a C-suite that turns out to be one guy behind a curtain.
A Christmas Carol is a three-step performance improvement plan.
Jurassic Park is a cautionary tale about skipping the risk committee.
The Princess and the Pea is the most important mattress review ever written.
Rapunzel is a nuanced look at a long-term lease with a very difficult landlord.
The Count of Monte Cristo is a 1,200-page revenge plan that could have been an email.
The Boy Who Cried Wolf is a landmark study in alert fatigue.
Hansel and Gretel is a cautionary tale about the free snacks at a recruiting event.
The Sun Also Rises is just a bachelor party that lasts an entire book.
Winnie-the-Pooh is a fearless investigation into one bear's honey supply chain.
The Secret Garden is a quietly ruthless story about a hostile takeover of the landscaping.
